\begin{abstract}
Aerial person detection is a core capability for search and rescue, yet the
datasets used to benchmark it were collected in calm, clear conditions,
while the missions that need it most take place during floods, wildfires,
storms, and at night. We present AegisBench, a robustness benchmark that
evaluates aerial search-and-rescue person detection under nine physically
motivated visual corruptions spanning four disaster families, each at three
severities calibrated by a declared image statistic. We evaluate three
architecturally distinct detectors, a two-stage CNN, a single-stage CNN, and
a transformer detector, across 168 conditions on two datasets covering the
high-altitude and low-altitude capture regimes, scoring every model with one
shared evaluator at operating points frozen on clean validation data.
Robustness is highly uneven, and unevenly so even for the same corruption
across datasets: heavy rain costs only about 3.6 points of recall at the
highest severity on SARD but drives recall to near zero on HERIDAL, while
low light is universal, producing complete detection collapse, recall
reaching exactly zero for all three architectures on both datasets, and
every one of 1,000 bootstrap resamples of the test set agrees, so the
confidence interval is degenerate at zero. A
localization-stability analysis shows that surviving detections remain
accurately placed, indicating that corruption causes missed detections
rather than positional drift. We release the benchmark, the corruption
engine, and the full evaluation pipeline.
\end{abstract}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Introduction}
% ---------------------------------------------------------------------

Aerial search and rescue depends on rapidly scanning wide, difficult terrain
for a missing person, and speed is the dominant factor in survival: the
first hours after a person goes missing are consistently the period in
which recovery is most likely. Automated person detection in aerial and
drone imagery has become a practical tool for this task, letting a single
operator or algorithm review coverage that would take a ground team days to
traverse. A detector that misses a person in the frame is not a benign
error; it is a missed rescue.

Published results on the two standard benchmarks for this task, HERIDAL and
SARD, report strong detection performance. Both datasets, however, were
collected in calm, clear, well-lit conditions. Real search-and-rescue
missions are launched precisely because something has gone wrong: after a
flood, during a wildfire, in a storm, or at night, when visibility is worst
and the need for automated coverage is greatest. No existing benchmark
systematically measures how aerial person detectors behave under the visual
conditions of the disasters that trigger these deployments. The gap between
a detector's benchmarked accuracy and its operational reliability is, at
present, simply unmeasured.

We address this gap with a benchmark that applies nine physically motivated
visual corruptions, spanning four disaster families (flood, wildfire,
storm, and earthquake), to the HERIDAL and SARD test sets, and evaluates
three architecturally distinct detectors across all resulting conditions.
Three design choices distinguish this from a straightforward transplant of
the ImageNet-C corruption-robustness methodology to aerial imagery. First,
each corruption is built on a documented optical model of a specific
disaster condition, such as the Koschmieder atmospheric scattering model
for smoke and dust, rather than a generic image-processing filter. Second,
each corruption's three severities are calibrated against a declared,
machine-verified image statistic, rather than chosen by eye. Third, every
detector's confidence threshold is selected once on clean validation data
and frozen across all corrupted conditions, matching how a system would
actually be deployed rather than measuring a best case unavailable in the
field.

The results show that robustness is highly uneven across conditions, and
unevenly so even for a single corruption across datasets. Heavy rain, at
its most severe, costs a detector only a few points of recall on SARD but
drives recall to near zero on HERIDAL. Low light is worse still and
universal: it drives recall to exactly zero, with bootstrap confidence
intervals degenerate at $[0.000, 0.000]$, on both datasets and for all
three architectures, a collapse confirmed independently of any confidence
threshold by mAP. A second robustness axis, localization
stability, shows that the detections a model does retain stay accurately
placed even as recall collapses: the dominant failure mode is a detector
ceasing to find a person, not finding one and misplacing the box.

Our contributions are:

\begin{itemize}
\item A disaster-grounded corruption benchmark for aerial search-and-rescue
  person detection: nine corruptions across four disaster families, each at
  three severities calibrated by a declared, measurable image statistic,
  applied to two datasets spanning the high- and low-altitude capture
  regimes, with every stochastic element seeded from a stable hash so the
  corrupted benchmark is a fixed, reproducible dataset rather than a random
  process.
\item A systematic robustness evaluation of three architecturally distinct
  detectors across 168 conditions, scored by one shared evaluator at
  operating points frozen on clean validation data, with bootstrap
  confidence intervals on the headline metrics, released as a full,
  provenance-logged pipeline.
\item The identification of catastrophic, cross-architecture detection
  collapse under low light, where recall reaches exactly zero with
  degenerate confidence intervals on both datasets and for all three
  detectors, alongside a severity ranking across all nine corruptions.
\item A localization-stability analysis that separates two failure modes
  normally conflated under a single recall number: losing a detection
  entirely, versus keeping it with a box that drifts off the person.
\end{itemize}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Related Work}
% ---------------------------------------------------------------------

\subsection{Aerial and Search-and-Rescue Person Detection}

Aerial search-and-rescue person detection is most often benchmarked on
HERIDAL~\cite{bozic2019heridal}, high-altitude orthophoto imagery of
wilderness terrain, and SARD~\cite{sambolek2021sard}, lower-altitude drone
video of staged rescue scenarios; both report strong detection accuracy
from CNN-based detectors trained and evaluated under calm, clear
conditions. Adjacent WACV benchmarks extend the small-person-in-large-scene
setting to other environments: TinyPerson~\cite{yu2020tinyperson} to
general tiny-object detection and SeaDronesSee~\cite{varga2022seadronessee}
to maritime search and rescue, both under similarly unconstrained visual
conditions.

The closest prior robustness evaluation on this exact data is the
SARD-Corr supplement released with SARD itself~\cite{sambolek2021sard},
which adds fog, snow, ice, and motion-blur variants to a subset of the
imagery. That supplement applies a small set of generic weather effects
without a calibrated severity structure and reports a single robustness
check rather than a systematic sweep. We extend this into a benchmark: nine
corruptions organized by disaster family, each at three severities
calibrated against a declared and machine-checked image statistic,
evaluated across three architecturally distinct detectors and two capture
regimes with bootstrap confidence intervals and a second,
localization-stability axis. Across all of this prior work, evaluation is
conducted exclusively under clear, undegraded conditions.

\subsection{Corruption Robustness Benchmarking}

Corruption-robustness benchmarking, established by
ImageNet-C~\cite{hendrycks2019imagenetc}, evaluates models under a fixed
suite of synthetic corruptions at graded severities. Michaelis et
al.~\cite{michaelis2019benchmarking} extended this methodology to object
detection in autonomous driving, applying generic corruptions to Pascal,
COCO, and Cityscapes; our domain (aerial small-object search and rescue
rather than street-level driving), our disaster-specific and physically
calibrated corruptions rather than generic transplants, and our
localization-stability axis all differ from that work, which remains the
closest methodological antecedent.

Robustness benchmarking for drone imagery under weather-like conditions has
become active only very recently. UAV-C~\cite{liu2024uavc} benchmarks UAV
\emph{tracking}, not detection, against eighteen generic corruptions
borrowed from the standard common-corruptions taxonomy.
HazyDet~\cite{feng2024hazydet} pairs physics-driven synthetic haze with
real foggy drone photographs for general object detection: one condition
rather than nine, and objects generally rather than search-and-rescue
persons specifically. WRRT-DETR~\cite{liu2025wrrtdetr} builds a
weather-robust RT-DETR variant around AWOD, a maritime dataset of imagery
captured under fog, flare, and low-light conditions. Each of these targets
a different task, a narrower corruption scope, or a different domain; none
combines physically grounded, disaster-specific corruption modeling with a
localization-stability axis that separates a detection lost entirely from
one that survives but drifts, which is what this benchmark adds beyond
breadth of coverage.

\subsection{Adverse Weather and Low-Light Vision}

Our physical corruption models draw on the atmospheric-optics and
low-light literature. Narasimhan and Nayar~\cite{narasimhan2002vision}
formalize the Koschmieder scattering model underlying our haze-family
corruptions. Chen et al.~\cite{chen2018dark} motivate modeling low light in
the linear photometric domain, which our \texttt{low\_light} corruption
follows. Garg and Nayar~\cite{garg2007rain} establish the physical
rain-streak model our \texttt{rain\_streaks} corruption adapts. Sakaridis
et al.~\cite{sakaridis2018foggy} apply synthetic fog to real driving
imagery, the closest methodological precedent for corrupting a real
dataset with a physical model, and later contribute real adverse-condition
data~\cite{sakaridis2021acdc}; dehazing~\cite{he2011dark} and low-light
enhancement~\cite{loh2019exdark} literature supports the same physical
models but restores images rather than measuring detector degradation.
This body of work is concentrated on autonomous driving and ground-level
imagery and on image restoration; none of it measures aerial person
detector degradation under these conditions directly.

\subsection{Small-Object Detection and Tiling}

People in HERIDAL-scale aerial imagery occupy a tiny fraction of a roughly
$4000\times3000$ frame, the regime that motivates tiled
inference~\cite{akyon2022sahi}: an image is cut into overlapping windows,
detected independently, and merged back to full-image coordinates. We
adopt this protocol for both datasets so that tiling is not itself a
confound when comparing degradation across the two capture regimes, and
evaluate throughout against full-image ground truth after
class-agnostic non-maximum-suppression merging.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Benchmark Design}
% ---------------------------------------------------------------------

Nine corruptions are organized into four disaster families: flood
(\texttt{water\_glare}, \texttt{turbidity\_cast}, \texttt{inundation}),
wildfire (\texttt{smoke\_haze}, \texttt{fire\_warm\_tint}), storm
(\texttt{rain\_streaks}, \texttt{motion\_blur}, \texttt{low\_light}), and
earthquake and post-disaster (\texttt{dust\_haze}). Each corruption models
a documented optical signature of its disaster family rather than a
generic image-processing filter (Table~\ref{tab:taxonomy},
Figure~\ref{fig:taxonomy}).

\paragraph{Physical models.} Three corruptions, \texttt{smoke\_haze} and
\texttt{fire\_warm\_tint} in the wildfire family and \texttt{dust\_haze} in
the earthquake family, are built on the Koschmieder atmospheric scattering
model~\cite{koschmieder1924theorie,narasimhan2002vision},
$I = J t + A(1-t)$, where $J$ is the clear-scene radiance, $A$ is the
atmospheric light, and $t$ is the transmission map. \texttt{smoke\_haze}
and \texttt{dust\_haze} differ principally in the chromaticity of $A$:
smoke uses a neutral-gray airlight, dust a brown mineral airlight,
consistent with the documented spectral difference between combustion
aerosol and suspended mineral particulate, and verified directly by a unit
test on the red-to-blue channel ratio of the two corruptions.
\texttt{fire\_warm\_tint} applies the same scattering model with a warm
airlight and a higher-frequency transmission field, preceded by a
white-balance shift toward orange modeling low-color-temperature
firelight.

The flood family is modeled differently, since sediment-laden water is not
an atmospheric scattering process. \texttt{turbidity\_cast} applies a blend
toward a mud chromaticity, compresses contrast toward the scene mean, and
reduces saturation, reproducing imagery dominated by muddy water rather
than by suspended aerosol. \texttt{low\_light} is modeled in the linear
photometric domain~\cite{chen2018dark} with a decode gamma of 2.2, photon
scaling, a twilight blue shift, and signal-dependent shot and read noise
whose relative magnitude grows as light falls. \texttt{rain\_streaks}
follows the additive directional-streak rain model of Garg and
Nayar~\cite{garg2007rain} over a blurred rain veil, and
\texttt{water\_glare} adds specular sun-glint saturation.

\subsection{Calibration and Severity}
\label{sec:calibration}

Each corruption declares a measurable image statistic in
\texttt{configs/corruptions.yaml} whose value must move monotonically
across severities one through three (Table~\ref{tab:taxonomy}). Severity
calibration is verified on a fixed random subset of 20 images drawn without
replacement from the HERIDAL test split, held constant across all nine
corruptions and all three severities. For each corruption and severity we
measure the declared statistic on every image in that subset and verify
that the subset mean moves in the declared direction; the same check runs
on synthetic imagery in the unit-test suite. This is a guarantee about the
mean over that subset, not about every individual image: the corruptions
are stochastic, so an individual image can invert without the severity
ladder being ill-formed.

Eight of nine corruptions pass this check directly. \texttt{rain\_streaks}
does not: its declared statistic, streak density, has no closed-form image
measure, so edge strength is substituted as a proxy, and the proxy is
confounded, since additional streaks raise measured edge strength while the
veil blur applied in the same corruption suppresses it.
\texttt{rain\_streaks}' severity is instead defined directly by its
physical generation parameters (streaks per megapixel, streak length, and
veil intensity, all increasing by construction; Table~\ref{tab:taxonomy})
and verified by visual audit; downstream recall degrades in the expected
direction regardless (Table~\ref{tab:spectrum}), independent evidence that
the corruption itself intensifies with severity even though this one proxy
statistic does not track it cleanly.

The calibration statistic makes each corruption's severity ladder
measurable and falsifiable \emph{within} that corruption. It is not a
cross-corruption difficulty normalizer: two corruptions matched on the same
statistic are not expected to be equally damaging, and we make no such
claim. \texttt{smoke\_haze} and \texttt{dust\_haze} illustrate this
directly: they reach nearly identical RMS contrast at every severity
(0.0475 versus 0.0489 at severity 3) yet differ 6.7-fold in cost
(Section~\ref{sec:results}), evidence that detection difficulty in this
domain is not reducible to global contrast reduction alone. We do not
isolate which of the two corruptions' remaining differences, airlight
chromaticity, transmission-field granularity, or added grain, carries the
effect.

\paragraph{Ground-truth alignment, scale invariance, and determinism.} All
pixel-unit generation parameters (blur kernel length, streak length, bloom
sigma, ripple amplitude) are specified per 1000 pixels of the longer image
side and scaled at runtime, so severity 2 means the same thing on a
$4000\times3000$ HERIDAL frame and a $640\times640$ SARD frame.
Corruptions are appearance-only: they recolor, darken, haze, or overlay the
existing pixel grid without moving object content, so clean ground-truth
boxes remain exactly valid on corrupted images. The one exception is
\texttt{inundation}, which applies a water-refraction ripple via pixel
remapping while the ground-truth box stays fixed; the ripple amplitude is
bounded well below person scale, reaching approximately 1.4 pixels at
severity 3 on a 4000-pixel frame, so residual misalignment is negligible.
Every stochastic element is seeded by a SHA-256-based stable hash of
$(\text{image\_id}, \text{corruption}, \text{severity}, \text{global\_seed})$,
independent of \texttt{PYTHONHASHSEED} and platform, so the corrupted
benchmark is a fixed dataset that regenerates bit-identically on any
machine, and we do not redistribute imagery: the code, the parameter
table, and this determinism are sufficient for anyone holding the original
datasets to reproduce every corrupted image exactly.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Evaluation Protocol}
% ---------------------------------------------------------------------

\paragraph{Frozen operating points.} Every detector needs a confidence
threshold to convert raw scores into detections. We select this threshold
once per model per dataset, by maximizing F1 on clean validation data, and
freeze it across all 28 conditions for that model (Table~\ref{tab:thresholds});
we never re-tune on corrupted data. A deployed system commits to one
threshold before a mission, and tuning per condition would measure a best
case unavailable to it.

\paragraph{Shared evaluator.} All three architectures are scored by one
evaluator: greedy, score-ordered matching at IoU $\geq 0.5$, one prediction
per ground-truth box, so no architecture is scored by a bespoke framework
metric.

\paragraph{Tiling and full-image evaluation.} Both datasets are processed
with the same tiling pipeline (1024-pixel tiles, 256-pixel overlap),
applied uniformly regardless of native resolution. A $4000\times3000$
HERIDAL frame exceeds the tile size and is split into 20 overlapping
tiles; each of SARD's $640\times640$ frames is smaller than the tile size
and is therefore passed through as a single full-frame tile. Detection
runs independently per tile, predicted boxes are mapped back into
full-image coordinates, and overlapping predictions are merged with
class-agnostic non-maximum suppression, so evaluation is always performed
against the original full-resolution ground truth rather than against
individual tiles. Applying one inference protocol, rather than a
hand-tuned one per dataset, removes an experimenter degree of freedom when
comparing degradation across capture regimes, though the resulting tiling
behavior itself differs by native resolution: HERIDAL frames are genuinely
tiled, SARD frames are not. At evaluation time, corruptions are applied to
the full frame before tiling, since atmospheric structure such as haze
gradients and flood masks is spatially coherent across a whole scene.

\paragraph{Relative performance drop.} Degradation is reported relative to
each model's own clean score, $\mathrm{rPD} = (\text{clean} -
\text{corrupted})/\text{clean}$, since HERIDAL and SARD do not share a
difficulty floor and raw corrupted metrics are not comparable across them.

\paragraph{Localization stability.} For instances detected in both the
clean and corrupted conditions, we measure the IoU between the two
predicted boxes, a scale-normalized center shift, and the drop in
box-versus-ground-truth fit. Restricting to commonly detected instances
means this metric is not confounded by recall: it asks whether a surviving
detection stayed planted on the person, a question distinct from whether
the person was found at all, in the tradition of prior detector
failure-mode decompositions~\cite{hoiem2012diagnosing,bolya2020tide}.

\paragraph{Bootstrap confidence intervals.} We resample the test set by
image with replacement, 1000 resamples per condition, and report the 2.5th
and 97.5th percentiles~\cite{efron1993bootstrap}.

\paragraph{Provenance.} Every result row logs the git commit, a hash of the
corruption configuration, the global seed, and a timestamp, and raw
per-condition predictions are archived, so any reported number is
traceable to the exact code and parameters that produced it and
re-analysis does not require rerunning inference.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Experimental Setup}
% ---------------------------------------------------------------------

We fine-tune three architecturally distinct detectors from pretrained
weights, one training run per model per dataset: Faster
R-CNN~\cite{ren2015fasterrcnn}, a two-stage CNN; YOLOv11~\cite{ultralytics2024yolo11},
a single-stage CNN; and RT-DETR~\cite{zhao2024rtdetr}, a transformer
detector in the DETR~\cite{carion2020detr} lineage. All three train at
1024-pixel input resolution (Table~\ref{tab:training}); hyperparameters
follow each architecture's established fine-tuning practice rather than a
shared schedule, and the two-order-of-magnitude difference in learning
rate between RT-DETR and the two CNN detectors follows this convention
rather than tuning against corrupted data, which never enters training or
threshold selection. Training uses a single consumer GPU (8~GB VRAM),
worth stating since it shows the benchmark is reproducible without a
cluster.

HERIDAL uses its official test split of 101 images untouched, with a
validation split carved deterministically from the official train split
(1391 train, 155 validation images, measured from our prepared records).
We use a Roboflow re-export of SARD, resized to $640\times640$; its
documented preprocessing applies no augmentation, only auto-orientation
and the resize, yet the export contains 5,755 images against SARD's
documented 1,981 source frames. Spot-checking colliding filenames shows
these are distinct frames, with different pixel content and different
annotations, that share a filename token, consistent with frame-counter
reuse across the mirror's upload history rather than duplicated or
augmented content. SARD frames originate from video, so temporally
adjacent frames are near-duplicates; splitting is group-aware, assigning
every image sharing a filename token to exactly one of train, validation,
or test, with the split tooling refusing degenerate groupings. We verified
directly that no filename-token group's images appear in more than one
split. SARD's test split used here contains 862 images (4033 train, 860
validation).

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}
% ---------------------------------------------------------------------

\subsection{Clean Baselines}

Table~\ref{tab:clean} reports clean-condition performance for all three
detectors on both datasets. On HERIDAL, our numbers sit modestly below the
commonly cited YOLOv5L reference point of roughly 0.90 precision, 0.893
recall, and 0.834 mAP$_{50}$~\cite{bozic2019heridal}, and are comparable in
mAP and precision; this order-of-magnitude agreement across different
architectures and input pipelines is the claim we make, not a superiority
claim. Clean recall is substantially higher on SARD (0.879 to 0.891) than
on HERIDAL (0.745 to 0.792), consistent with SARD's lower-altitude capture
and larger relative object size making it the easier detection task.
Because the two datasets do not share a difficulty floor, every
degradation result below is reported as relative drop against each model's
own clean score rather than as a raw corrupted metric.

\subsection{Robustness Across Conditions}

Table~\ref{tab:spectrum} and Figure~\ref{fig:severity} report recall by
corruption and severity for YOLOv11 on SARD. Robustness is highly uneven.
At matched severity 3, recall ranges from 0.855 for \texttt{rain\_streaks},
a 3.6-point drop from the 0.891 clean baseline, to exactly 0.000 for
\texttt{low\_light}, a total loss. This range, produced by corruptions
calibrated on comparable statistical ladders (Table~\ref{tab:taxonomy}),
is the argument that this benchmark is diagnostic rather than merely hard:
a single averaged robustness score would collapse the entire finding into
one number and hide it.

Table~\ref{tab:family} aggregates relative recall drop by disaster family.
Flood is the mildest family on both datasets for every model without
exception, the one family-level ordering fully consistent across the
study. Storm is worst on HERIDAL, pulled up by \texttt{low\_light}'s
collapse; earthquake (\texttt{dust\_haze}) is worst on SARD.
Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} shows the same pattern per corruption: the
\texttt{low\_light} row saturates for all three architectures.

\subsection{Detection Collapse Under Low Light}

\texttt{low\_light} is the benchmark's headline result
(Table~\ref{tab:lowlight}). By severity 3, recall reaches exactly 0.000
for all three architectures on both HERIDAL ($n=101$) and SARD ($n=862$),
and every one of 1{,}000 bootstrap resamples of the test set agrees: the
confidence interval is degenerate at $[0.000, 0.000]$. A two-stage CNN, a
single-stage CNN, and a transformer detector are about as architecturally
different as detectors get, and by severity 3 all three sit at exactly the
same floor, which rules out an architecture-specific explanation.

A natural objection is that a frozen-threshold zero reflects a badly placed
operating point rather than a genuine failure to detect.
Table~\ref{tab:calibration} settles this with mAP$_{50}$, which scans every
confidence threshold and is therefore immune to the objection: on HERIDAL
at severity 1, RT-DETR's mAP$_{50}$ collapses from 0.835 clean to 0.001,
YOLOv11's from 0.803 to 0.064, and Faster R-CNN's from 0.785 to 0.537, in
lockstep with frozen-threshold recall. If this were a calibration
artifact, mAP would stay high while recall fell; it does not, so the
detections are absent rather than merely below threshold.

As an independent check outside our synthetic pipeline entirely, we ran
the SARD-trained YOLOv11 model, unmodified, on 40 real nighttime images
from VisDrone~\cite{zhu2021visdrone}, an unrelated aerial-imagery
benchmark, selected as the lowest-luminance images in its test split and
manually confirmed to depict genuine dusk or night scenes. Recall against
VisDrone's own person annotations was 0.016 (2 of 128 ground-truth boxes
recovered), comparable to our synthetic severity 1 and close to the
severity 3 collapse. This is a small, uncontrolled sample from a different
capture domain (lit urban scenes rather than SAR wilderness terrain), not
a substitute for systematic real-condition validation, but it is
independent evidence that the collapse we report is not an artifact of
our corruption pipeline.

Two claims are safe across both datasets: total collapse by severity 3
replicates for all three architectures, and Faster R-CNN is consistently
the most robust of the three at low light, on both datasets, at every
severity where any model retains recall, despite having the strictest
frozen threshold (0.99 on HERIDAL, versus 0.65 for RT-DETR and 0.45 for
YOLOv11), which rules out threshold strictness as the explanation. One
claim is not safe: RT-DETR is the most fragile architecture on HERIDAL
(zero recall at every severity, including the mildest), but this reverses
on SARD, where RT-DETR outperforms YOLOv11 at severities 1 and 2. The
ordering between YOLOv11 and RT-DETR is dataset-dependent, not an
architecture property, and we state it as such.

\subsection{Localization Stability}

Figure~\ref{fig:decoupling} plots recall against localization stability
for YOLOv11 on SARD, one point per corruption and severity. Both axes span
the full unit range deliberately: stability declines from 0.98 to 0.78
across the severity range while recall falls from 0.89 to 0.00, so both
quantities do decline, and we do not claim they are independent. The claim
the data supports is one of magnitude: recall sweeps nearly the entire
unit range while stability stays inside a narrow band near the top, never
falling below 0.78 even in conditions that remove almost every detection,
while $n_{\text{common}}$, the number of instances detected in both
conditions, tracks recall exactly (\texttt{low\_light}: 202, then 8, then
0). The dominant failure mode is a detection disappearing, not a box
drifting off the person. Figure~\ref{fig:qualitative} shows this directly:
a clean HERIDAL frame beside the same frame under \texttt{low\_light},
where every annotated person goes undetected. Operationally, if surviving
detections stay accurately placed, the risk for a deployed system lies in
the detections that never appear rather than in ones that appear
misplaced, which also indicates what a mitigation should target:
sensitivity rather than localization.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Limitations}
% ---------------------------------------------------------------------

Our corruptions are synthetic, applied to real imagery, following the
ImageNet-C and Foggy Cityscapes
lineage~\cite{hendrycks2019imagenetc,sakaridis2018foggy}, a limitation
shared by the corruption-robustness methodology broadly and not unique to
this benchmark. This is what makes controlled, per-condition attribution
possible at all, since disaster imagery rarely comes with a matched clean
counterpart of the same scene, but it is also the benchmark's ceiling: it
measures response to modeled optics, not to live disaster footage; a
small spot check against real night imagery (Section~\ref{sec:results})
is suggestive but not a substitute for systematic validation against real
adverse-condition SAR footage, which remains a natural next step, made
harder by how rarely such footage is collected and released. We train one
seed per
model per dataset; our bootstrap intervals quantify variance from which
images are in the test set, not from training. We evaluate two datasets
and three detectors, prioritizing methodological depth, physically
grounded corruption modeling, group-aware splitting, frozen-threshold
evaluation, and bootstrap confidence intervals over dataset and model
count, consistent with a diagnostic benchmark rather than a leaderboard
survey. \texttt{rain\_streaks}' declared statistic has no closed-form
image measure and its substituted proxy is confounded by the corruption's
own veil blur (Section~\ref{sec:calibration}); severity is instead defined
by monotonically increasing generation parameters and verified by visual
audit. Monotonicity is verified on a fixed random 20-image subset by its
mean, not per image, since the corruptions are stochastic.
\texttt{inundation}'s ripple leaves ground-truth boxes unwarped, with
negligible amplitude ($\approx$1.4 pixels at severity 3 on a 4000-pixel
frame). Finally, we run no mitigation study. Disaster-aware training
augmentation, targeted first at the low-light collapse identified here, is
the natural next experiment, for which stylization-based augmentation is
independent precedent~\cite{michaelis2019benchmarking}; the pipeline for
it is released, but a rushed result before this submission's deadline
would be worse than none.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Conclusion}
% ---------------------------------------------------------------------

Aerial search-and-rescue person detection is benchmarked on calm, clear
imagery and deployed into disasters. We measure the gap directly:
robustness across nine physically grounded, disaster-family corruptions is
highly uneven, and unevenly so even for the same corruption across
datasets: heavy rain costs a few points of recall on SARD but nearly all
of it on HERIDAL, while low light collapses recall to exactly zero on both
datasets and for all three architecturally distinct detectors, confirmed
independently of any confidence threshold. Surviving detections stay accurately placed even as
recall collapses, so the failure mode is a detector going blind rather
than misplacing what it finds. Systems intended for disaster response
should be evaluated under disaster conditions, and current detectors carry
a specific, measurable, architecture-independent blind spot at exactly the
low-light conditions where aerial search is most valuable and least
substitutable by ground teams. Disaster-aware training augmentation is the
natural mitigation and our immediate next experiment; we do not claim
generality beyond the two datasets and three architectures evaluated here.

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Ethical Considerations}
% ---------------------------------------------------------------------

We use only publicly available research datasets, obtained from their
original distributors under those datasets' own terms, and collect no new
human-subjects data. SARD consists of staged imagery in which volunteers
simulate lost or injured persons; HERIDAL contains aerial imagery of
people in wilderness terrain. We add no new imagery and no new annotations
of people, and annotate no identity, biometric, or demographic attribute:
persons appear only as generic bounding boxes inherited from the source
datasets. We redistribute no imagery. Because every corruption is
deterministically seeded, the corrupted benchmark regenerates exactly from
the clean datasets, so reproduction requires only the released code and
the original datasets under their own licenses.
